analysis.one_liner: Caps U.S. prices of taxpayer-funded drugs at what other wealthy countries pay.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Energy and Commerce Committee; after its May 2023 referral, no hearing, markup, or vote ever occurred before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies that develop a drug, vaccine, device, or diagnostic with federal research money would have to sign an agreement with the Health and Human Services Secretary to charge a 'reasonable' price. The bill defines reasonable as no more than the median price in Canada and six other large, high-income countries, and requires companies to publicly report their clinical trial costs, federal subsidies, and annual sales revenue. The Secretary could waive the price limit only after public notice, comment, and a published economic analysis.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who need drugs, vaccines, medical devices, or tests built on federally funded research. Today, taxpayers often pay twice: once to fund the science, then again at the pharmacy counter, where U.S. prices for the same products commonly run far above what people in Canada and other wealthy countries pay. The bill would tie U.S. prices to the median of those countries and force disclosure of the true public cost behind each product.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every federal research agreement and every license on a resulting patent or test data to include a reasonable-pricing obligation, so federally funded inventions cannot be priced without limit [S3].

Sets the U.S. price ceiling at the median price in Canada and six other large, high-income OECD economies, ensuring Americans do not pay more than people in comparable countries for the same product [S3].

Requires manufacturers to report clinical trial costs, federal subsidies of those costs, and annual revenues, and makes those reports publicly available, giving the public a look at what it actually paid to develop a product [S3].

Allows the Secretary to adopt stronger mechanisms, such as lowering prices or shortening exclusivity when revenues exceed targets, while any waiver of the price limit requires public notice, a hearing, comment, and a published economic analysis [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies, and to a lesser extent universities and research institutions that license federally funded patents, would see revenue capped on products built with federal money. Companies argue lower returns would shrink private investment in new drug development, since the bill also requires regulators to weigh the importance of robust research incentives.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies only to products developed with federal funding, so most marketed drugs from company-funded research would be untouched, and the Secretary's public-interest waiver could carve out exceptions case by case [S3].

Companies and many economists argue that capping prices on federally supported inventions would reduce expected returns and slow private investment in bringing laboratory discoveries to patients; the bill itself instructs regulators to weigh that risk in any rules it writes [S3].

Determining a price for a federally funded 'product or service' is administratively difficult when patents, know-how, or assets are controlled by third parties, a challenge the bill acknowledges but only addresses through future rulemaking [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea addresses a real, widely recognized problem: the federal government funds early-stage biomedical research and then permits companies to charge Americans more than anyone else in the developed world for the results. The benefit would fall on millions of patients who use federally supported products, while the cost falls on a concentrated industry. The main honest objection is that a hard price ceiling could dull incentives to commercialize federally funded discoveries, and the bill's reach is limited to federally funded work. On balance, a pricing guarantee tied to peer-country prices plus public disclosure of development costs is a stronger deal for taxpayers than the status quo.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2025 without a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Val Hoyle introduced the bill on May 5, 2023, with 14 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced [S5].
A week later it was referred to the subcommittee on Health, and no further action of any kind is recorded for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill ended the 118th Congress without a committee vote or a floor vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug and biotech companies that commercialize federally funded research are better off: they keep charging U.S. prices above peer countries with no pricing obligation attached to public funding. Taxpayers continue funding the research without a guarantee of affordable access to the results.

for.name: Rep. Val Hoyle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and attached a reasonable-pricing requirement to federally funded biomedical research.

for.name: 18 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup; the bill went to the Health Subcommittee on May 12, 2023, and the record shows no further action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support recorded; the committee that controlled the bill's fate was run by Republicans, and no vote ever took place [S4, S5].

industries.note: The bill would cap prices of drugs, vaccines, devices, and tests developed with federal research money at the median price of peer countries, and require public reporting of development costs and revenues. It would end the current arrangement in which taxpayers fund the science and companies then charge U.S. patients more than anyone else in the developed world.

industries.industry: Universities and nonprofit research institutions licensing federally funded patents
industries.note: Institutions holding licenses on federally funded inventions would face the same pricing and reporting obligations and potentially lower royalty streams, while the bill preserves the existing tech-transfer system under Bayh-Dole rather than replacing it.
